body:
Where I land is a revision, not a choice among the three inputs. The account's remedy largely survives the objection; its diagnosis and its test do not. The rival's diagnosis is the best mechanism offered for the avoidance; its proposed opening move is not. Here is what I take up, change, or decline, and why.

From the objection I take the central point in full strength: later disagreement about what an agreement meant is consistent with at least three distinguishable readings — ambiguity about the words, renegotiation about whether terms still bind after a schedule change, and legitimacy about who may raise and enforce a miss. My ground for adopting this is that the readings are remedy-bearing. Criteria for done-ness and timing address only the first, and here the account is stronger than it claimed: its own third column, "what happens when someone cannot do it," is exactly a renegotiation clause. The objection's example — "yes, and then my shift changed" — is what a fallback rule handles. So the spec probe covers two readings even though the account argued for one. Neither column touches legitimacy; if the live dispute is about standing, clearer paperwork arms the enforcer and sharpens the dispute. I adopt the objection's three readings as rivals, keep the spec probe, and stop claiming it covers the field.

I also take the objection's attack on the test: whether two or three specified items stop recurring does not discriminate. But the rival supplies the missing instrument, and it can be extended. What discriminates is the pattern of failure, not the rate. If specified items settle while complaints migrate to the next unspecified item, the supply of grievance is the problem — relational or legitimacy reading. If specs hold until the next schedule change and then break, renegotiation reading. If the items are done yet policing fights continue, legitimacy or load. If the withdrawing flatmate engages with the content of a proposed spec — argues about what should count as done — ambiguity gains support; if they pull back from the very idea of a written arrangement, the rival's reading does. One probe observed this way answers the objection's demand that it be built to tell rivals apart, not merely to count recurrence.

From the rival I take the core conjecture: the disputes may be about whether the flat is a unit with obligations or three private lives sharing fixtures. This best explains the distinctive fact in the material — the avoidance — because it predicts withdrawal from any settled term, not from vague ones. I also take the truce-shaped arrangements (owned zones, rotations with a default outcome, no audit) as the remedy matched to the privacy and legitimacy readings, where specification is the wrong tool. And I keep the rival's own self-objection: the privacy reading can shield someone who simply does not want a share of the work. That caution sits symmetrically with the objection's warning that tighter specs on a lopsided arrangement remain lopsided. Each remedy enacts a side; neither reading is innocent, so neither should be installed as the frame before it has survived contact with the flatmates.

What I decline is the rival's opening move as first step: separate conversations about what the flatmates take the flat to be. My ground is behavioral. The one thing known about the withdrawing flatmate is that they exit conversations, and the household-identity question is the most abstract, highest-stakes version of the conversation there is — it asks the most of the person least likely to give it. Instead I retain the account's small, separate, low-pressure one-to-one but change its content: not "ten minutes on the bins" with a spec agenda folded inside, and not "what kind of household is this," but "when we end up arguing about the bins, what do you think the argument is actually about?" That is concrete enough to answer, small enough not to be fled, and the answer — plus the manner of answering — is diagnostic across all four readings at once. Chore content advances the spec probe. "It's not the bins, it's that I'm always the one" advances truce-shaped arrangements as the honest next offer. Refusal of the question itself advances the rival's reading, and the flat-shape conversations then come earlier than planned — conducted separately and never aggregated into a group settlement, per the rival's own commitment.

One caution neither input made: the person asking is one of the three flatmates, not a mediator, and may already be cast as the enforcer. That contaminates the rival's discriminator — pullback from a written note you proposed is data about you as much as about the note. The instrument survives, but readings from the asker's own probes should be discounted for authorship effects, and where feasible the proposal should be allowed to emerge as the pair's idea or the other flatmate's.

What survives from the account nearly as written: no single big settle-everything meeting, no moral language, no counting instances. The escalation threshold also survives, and the objection's worry that it arrives too late is partly answered by the rival's truce stage, which adds an earlier fork. All three sources converge on naming the living-arrangement question rather than deferring it; I make the threshold less passive — it is crossed when the low-pressure moves have been tried through one full schedule cycle without engagement, and when crossed it should be said aloud. I do not treat the objection's self-objection as collapsing its critique: even if ambiguity is the plainest reading, the objection's two substantive points — sequencing and the weakness of the recurrence test — stand on their own.

Left open: almost everything the objection's problem record listed — what the chores are, how long this has run, whether the withdrawing flatmate has ever said why — plus one more: whether the probes themselves become the next thing argued about. The mitigation is the account's original instinct, now recast as method rather than hunch: every move small, time-limited, and labeled a trial.
